paragraphs: Graph neural networks differ in which graph structures they can distinguish. Standard message passing has a known ceiling, described by the one-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman test. More powerful versions of that test inspire stronger networks, but their computational costs grow quickly. This paper asks how to increase expressive power in smaller, more practical steps.

The proposed hierarchy works with sets of nodes instead of ordered tuples. Two parameters control which sets are considered: k limits their size, and c limits the number of connected components they contain in the original graph. The authors establish theoretical relationships with the existing hierarchy and construct a neural network that matches the expressiveness of their new test.

Increasing k and c increases the model's power, providing finer control over the tradeoff between structural discrimination and computation. Experiments report several state-of-the-art benchmark results with practical runtime and memory use. The contribution is therefore both a way to measure intermediate levels of expressiveness and an architecture that makes those levels usable.
neurips-2022-a-practical-progressively-e.tldr: A graph neural network built around bounded node sets increases expressiveness gradually while keeping computation practical.

paragraphs: A neural network's Lipschitz constant describes how strongly its outputs can change when its inputs change. Estimating this quantity matters when controlling smoothness. An overly loose estimate can impose excessive regularization during training and hurt accuracy, making precision practically consequential rather than merely a mathematical preference.

The paper develops a unified geometric framework for studying these estimates. It yields theoretical results about computational difficulty and how well the quantity can be approximated. The same framework also produces algorithms based on semidefinite programming, connecting the theoretical analysis to procedures that can actually estimate network smoothness.

For perturbations measured with the infinity norm, the empirical evaluation finds these algorithms more precise and scalable than existing tools. The authors also examine their relationships with other semidefinite programming approaches, both mathematically and experimentally. The stated contribution is a common perspective that organizes existing techniques and supports improved estimation; the reported computational advantages concern the evaluated perturbation setting.
neurips-2022-a-quantitative-geometric-ap.tldr: A geometric framework yields theoretical insights and more scalable, precise empirical estimates of neural-network smoothness for infinity-norm perturbations.

paragraphs: Face-recognition attacks often modify individual pixels under a constraint on perturbation size. The authors identify two weaknesses of these approaches: attacks may transfer poorly between recognition models, and denoising defenses may remove their effect. They investigate whether changing higher-level facial attributes can produce attacks that remain visually inconspicuous while transferring more effectively.

Adv-Attribute introduces adversarial changes through semantic attributes. Differences between the recognition features of a face and those of a target guide these changes. The framework also selects attributes according to their importance and uses multiple optimization objectives to balance attack strength against how noticeable the resulting image changes are.

Experiments on FFHQ and CelebA-HQ report state-of-the-art attack success rates together with better visual results than recent attack methods. These findings support the paper's central proposal that semantic attributes are a useful space for constructing face-recognition attacks. The contribution joins attack effectiveness and visual subtlety in one framework, with the reported evidence coming from the two evaluated datasets.
neurips-2022-adv-attribute-inconspicuous.tldr: Adv-Attribute modifies semantic facial attributes to produce visually subtle attacks with strong reported success and transferability.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning lets several prediction tasks share model parameters, potentially reducing storage while improving accuracy. Making this work requires deciding which parameters should be shared. It also creates an engineering burden: applying a multi-task method to a different convolutional backbone can require substantial manual implementation and expertise.

AutoMTL addresses both issues through a programming framework. Its inputs are a convolutional neural network backbone and the tasks to learn. It automatically produces a multi-task model intended to combine high task accuracy with a small memory footprint. This makes the choice of parameter sharing part of an automated development process.

Experiments on CityScapes, NYUv2, and Tiny-Taskonomy demonstrate the framework's effectiveness relative to state-of-the-art approaches and its ability to work across different convolutional networks. The contribution matters because efficient sharing and ease of adoption are connected: a useful sharing strategy becomes more accessible when developers can apply it to their backbone without repeatedly rebuilding the method by hand.
neurips-2022-automtl-a-programming-frame.tldr: AutoMTL automates the construction of shared multi-task vision models that combine strong accuracy with a small memory footprint.

paragraphs: A coreset is a compact collection of representative data used in place of a much larger dataset. For Bayesian inference, the aim is to preserve statistically relevant information while making subsequent computation faster. Existing variational approaches either choose observed examples or optimize artificial examples that summarize the original data.

The paper identifies obstacles that make these methods difficult to apply broadly. Their optimization objectives can be complicated to evaluate, and they require samples from a posterior distribution over the coreset that is usually intractable. Those requirements can undermine the usefulness of data compression when the underlying probabilistic model is itself difficult to analyze.

The authors introduce a black-box variational inference framework designed to overcome these constraints and extend principled coreset methods to models such as Bayesian neural networks. They apply it to supervised learning and compare it with existing summarization and inference approaches. The central contribution is broader applicability of variational coresets, allowing compact data summaries to support inference in settings where earlier constructions were computationally awkward.
neurips-2022-black-box-coreset-variation.tldr: A black-box variational framework makes Bayesian coreset construction applicable to difficult models such as Bayesian neural networks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how network depth changes robust linear regression when some measurements are severely corrupted. The setting is over-parameterized, and an N-layer diagonal linear network represents the underlying linear model. Although additional layers create a nonconvex optimization problem, the authors investigate whether they can also produce useful behavior near the true solution.

The analysis first establishes a difficulty: at any depth, there is a constant probability of a parameter solution representing the ground truth that is neither a local nor a global minimum. Representing the correct model therefore does not automatically make a point favorable under the training objective.

For networks with at least two layers, however, the authors prove that a simple subgradient method avoids these problematic solutions and converges to a balanced solution near the truth with a flat local landscape. In this setting, early stopping is unnecessary. Experiments also find favorable landscape behavior in deep matrix recovery and ReLU networks trained with an absolute-error loss, extending the empirical evidence beyond the linear analysis.
neurips-2022-blessing-of-depth-in-linear.tldr: In a robust diagonal linear-network setting, depth enables subgradient training to reach flat solutions near the truth despite problematic ground-truth parameterizations.

paragraphs: GAN generators can produce realistic images with controllable variation, suggesting that their internal features contain useful information about image content. This paper explores how to transfer that information to a student network for downstream tasks. The goal is to make the generator's learned representations useful beyond image synthesis itself.

The first step, called squeeze, processes generator features through a network before distilling them into the student. It produces representations that remain unchanged under transformations preserving semantic content. This prepares the generator's knowledge for transfer by emphasizing information that should stay consistent when an image changes without changing its meaning.

The second step, span, incorporates real training data to extend learning from generated images to the real-image domain. It addresses the generator's mode collapse, which can leave parts of the real data distribution poorly represented. Experiments support the effectiveness of the combined approach for self-supervised representation learning. Together, the two steps address both the form of the transferred features and the coverage of the data used to learn them.
neurips-2022-distilling-representations-.tldr: Squeeze and Span transfers GAN-generator knowledge into a student using semantic invariance and real data to improve representation learning.

paragraphs: An observer may expect a reinforcement-learning agent to behave one way and then see it act differently. This paper treats explanation as a way to reconcile that discrepancy. Complex environments and decision procedures make the task difficult, while existing approaches often depend on domain expertise, policy analysis, or selected parts of the environment model.

The authors propose using transformations and abstractions of the environment's Markov decision process to generate explanations automatically. Such operations have previously helped search for optimal policies. Here, their typically symbolic representation provides a basis for expressing meaningful changes that explain the gap between anticipated and observed behavior.

A central claim is that the environment model can still help when it is only partially known or when the agent uses a model-free method and does not maintain one. The paper formally defines the explanation problem, introduces a class of suitable transformations, and develops methods for efficient explanation search. Demonstrations on standard benchmarks show the approach in use, connecting model-based reasoning to explanations of agents that need not themselves be model-based.
neurips-2022-explainable-reinforcement-l.tldr: Transforming environment models can automatically explain unexpected reinforcement-learning behavior, even when an agent lacks a complete model.

paragraphs: Some transformations should leave a model's prediction unchanged, such as rotations or translations in suitable application domains. This paper asks whether knowing these invariances can strengthen mathematical guarantees that predictions resist input perturbations. It connects a model's built-in treatment of symmetry with the task of certifying robustness.

The proposed approach adds knowledge about invariances to randomized smoothing, a technique ordinarily used without inspecting model structure. The authors call this combination gray-box certification. Their first construction uses group orbits, collections of inputs related by the relevant transformations, and applies to models invariant under permutations and Euclidean isometries.

The authors then derive provably tight certificates within their gray-box framework. Experiments show that these tight certificates can give substantially stronger guarantees, while the orbit-based construction provides a good approximation in practical scenarios. The findings establish that known symmetries can be useful evidence for certification, beyond their role in model design. The applicability of the guarantees depends on the model possessing the invariances used by the certificate.
neurips-2022-invariance-aware-randomized.tldr: Incorporating known model invariances into randomized smoothing can produce stronger provable robustness guarantees.

paragraphs: Neural networks are often organized as a sequence of layers, yet biological systems also contain parallel computational pathways. Such pathways might specialize because they pursue different objectives. This paper investigates another possibility: specialization could emerge even when every pathway is trained using the same objective.

The authors analyze learning in deep linear networks with large hidden layers. They describe features of the training data through the singular values of the input-output correlation, providing a mathematical way to track what the pathways learn. As pathway depth increases, different features typically become concentrated in individual pathways rather than being shared across them.

The result is derived analytically and supported by numerical simulations. It shows how parallel architecture and learning dynamics can produce sharply differentiated representations without assigning separate tasks to the pathways. The biological relevance is presented as a possible implication: the same mechanism may help explain specialized codes in biological and artificial systems. The established analysis itself uses the stated deep-linear, large-hidden-layer approximation.
neurips-2022-learning-dynamics-of-deep-l.tldr: Deep parallel linear pathways can specialize in different data features despite being trained with a shared objective.

paragraphs: In many reinforcement-learning problems, an action combines several smaller choices. Treating every combination as unrelated can make rarely observed combinations difficult to evaluate. This is especially relevant in offline learning, where an agent must learn from an existing dataset and may have little evidence for large parts of the action space.

The paper proposes a linear decomposition of the Q-function, which estimates action value, based on this structure of component actions. The authors identify settings in which the approximation has zero bias. These guarantees establish circumstances where factoring the value estimate does not introduce systematic approximation error.

Outside those settings, the method can still improve sample efficiency without necessarily losing policy optimality, offering a useful bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on simulated problems and real datasets motivated by healthcare show that incorporating action structure can produce better policies. The findings support using relationships between component choices to improve estimates in underexplored regions, while preserving the distinction between settings with theoretical guarantees and those supported empirically.
neurips-2022-leveraging-factored-action-.tldr: Decomposing action values around component choices can improve offline reinforcement learning, with zero-bias guarantees in identified settings.

paragraphs: Differential privacy can be expressed through the difficulty of distinguishing datasets in a hypothesis test. In this formulation, a canonical noise distribution provides additive noise that meets a specified privacy tradeoff without wasting privacy budget. The paper studies when such distributions can have two additional useful properties.

Log-concave noise supports an ordered relationship between inputs and outputs, so higher released values correspond to higher input values. Multivariate canonical noise supports a tight privacy description when several outputs are released jointly. The authors connect the existence and construction of these distributions to whether the privacy tradeoff can be decomposed through functional composition or mechanism composition.

They prove that pure epsilon differential privacy admits neither decomposition and has neither a log-concave canonical noise distribution nor a multivariate one. Gaussian differential privacy, zero-epsilon approximate privacy, and Laplace differential privacy admit both kinds. These results distinguish privacy formulations by which tightly matched additive mechanisms they permit; the negative result specifically concerns canonical noise with the stated properties.
neurips-2022-log-concave-and-multivariat.tldr: The paper characterizes when privacy tradeoffs permit log-concave or multivariate canonical noise, proving contrasting results for different privacy formulations.

paragraphs: Medical image segmentation assigns parts of an image to a target region, whose volume can be an important property of the result. This paper studies optimal segmentations under two common evaluation metrics, Accuracy and Dice, when target labels are noisy. It examines both what the optimal solutions look like and how much volume they contain.

The authors prove that optimizing either metric can produce a volume substantially different from the expected target volume. They also establish an ordering: an Accuracy-optimal solution has volume no greater than a Dice-optimal solution. Thus, the choice of metric has a systematic relationship with predicted volume, even when each solution is optimal for its own criterion.

A further result identifies a condition under which the metrics agree. If feasible segmentations must have volume equal to the expected target volume, their optimal solutions coincide. Experiments accompany the theoretical statements. Together, the findings show why metric optimality alone does not ensure volume agreement with a noisy target, and how a specific volume constraint reconciles the two objectives.
neurips-2022-on-image-segmentation-with-.tldr: With noisy segmentation labels, Accuracy and Dice can favor different volumes, but their optima coincide under an expected-target-volume constraint.

paragraphs: Learning fair predictions becomes challenging when data contains many subgroups and each subgroup has few examples. The paper seeks to reduce prediction disparities under the criterion of group sufficiency while retaining the predictive usefulness of the data. Its focus is on learning a shared predictor that accounts for all of these subgroups.

The method uses an objective with two linked levels. At the lower level, each subgroup gets a predictor learned from its limited data together with the shared fair predictor. At the upper level, the shared predictor is updated to stay close to the subgroup-specific predictors. The two levels connect subgroup adaptation with the construction of a common model.

The authors prove that this objective can control both group sufficiency and generalization error. Evaluations on real-world datasets suggest consistently improved fairness with accuracy comparable to the baselines. The approach therefore offers a principled way to connect fairness and predictive performance when subgroup data is scarce, with empirical findings supporting that balance in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2022-on-learning-fairness-and-ac.tldr: A bilevel learning objective connects subgroup-specific predictors to a shared model, improving reported fairness while maintaining comparable accuracy.

paragraphs: Generalization theory often analyzes training as if model parameters eventually settle at a fixed point. The paper addresses a mismatch with observed deep-learning behavior: stochastic gradient descent can leave weights oscillating indefinitely. It asks how to understand performance on unseen data when there may be no final, stationary parameter vector.

The authors introduce statistical algorithmic stability, extending classical stability to algorithms whose dynamics do not converge. Their approach draws on ergodic theory and examines the algorithm's long-term statistical behavior. This shifts the object of analysis from a single limiting solution to properties of the continuing training process.

They prove a relationship between stability of time-asymptotic behavior and generalization. Empirical results further show that loss dynamics can provide clues about performance beyond the training data. Together, the findings support the idea that stable training behavior can accompany better generalization even when individual weights never settle. The contribution is a framework for studying that situation, rather than requiring parameter convergence before generalization can be analyzed.
neurips-2022-on-the-generalization-of-le.tldr: Statistical algorithmic stability connects long-term training behavior to generalization even when network weights never converge.

paragraphs: An autonomous agent in an unfamiliar environment needs to interpret sensory observations, learn from experience, and plan over long horizons. PALMER combines learned perceptual representations with classical sampling-based planning to address these needs together. Its design uses past experience as material for constructing future plans.

The representation is trained through Q-learning and contrastive learning. Distances between state embeddings are intended to reflect how easily an optimal policy can travel between those states. This gives the planner a representation organized around movement through the environment, connecting perceptual similarity with the action requirements of reaching a destination.

For planning, PALMER retrieves previously observed trajectory segments from a replay buffer and stitches them into approximately optimal routes between start and goal states. Reusing these segments connects memory, representation learning, reinforcement learning, and classical planning in a feedback loop. The authors report substantially greater robustness and sample efficiency than existing methods. The key idea is to make learned perception and stored experience directly usable by a long-horizon planning procedure.
neurips-2022-palmer-perception-action-lo.tldr: PALMER combines learned reachability representations with remembered trajectory segments and sampling-based planning for robust, sample-efficient long-horizon navigation.

paragraphs: Complex-valued neural networks offer potentially richer representations and attractive theoretical properties, but their training behavior relative to ordinary real-valued networks is less understood. This paper investigates whether commonly used real-valued backpropagation preserves distinctive complex-network dynamics. The analysis focuses on the limit where network widths become infinite.

The authors extend the Tensor Program framework to complex numbers. They use it to show that the training dynamics of basic complex architectures under real-valued backpropagation are governed by their neural tangent kernels. Comparing these kernels then provides a mathematical route to comparing complex and real networks during training.

For most complex activation functions, the authors prove that the limiting training dynamics reduce to those of ordinary real networks. In that regime, the training procedure removes the distinctive dynamics that complex-valued computation might otherwise provide. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings. The conclusion is specifically about the studied backpropagation procedure and infinite-width behavior, making the interaction between representation and training method central to the result.
neurips-2022-real-valued-backpropagation.tldr: For most complex activations, real-valued backpropagation makes infinite-width complex networks train like ordinary real networks.

paragraphs: Long-tailed recognition learns from data where some classes are much more common than others. Many methods assume evaluation will give every class equal frequency. This paper studies a broader setting in which the test distribution is unknown and may remain long-tailed or even favor classes that were rare during training.

The proposed method trains multiple experts from the same fixed training dataset. These experts develop different skills for handling different class distributions. At test time, a self-supervised aggregation strategy combines their outputs to address the unknown class frequencies, linking diverse training-time expertise to adaptation during evaluation.

The authors theoretically establish that their self-supervised strategy can simulate test-agnostic class distributions. Experiments report promising results on both conventional and test-agnostic long-tailed recognition. The contribution addresses two connected problems: unequal training data and an unknown change in class frequencies at deployment. Its significance lies in preparing and combining different experts instead of building the entire recognition strategy around a uniform test distribution.
neurips-2022-self-supervised-aggregation.tldr: Diverse experts and self-supervised test-time aggregation help long-tailed recognition adapt to unknown test class distributions.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning often trains representations through a pretext task and then transfers them to other tasks. The authors argue that such task choices introduce biases that affect transfer. Maximum Entropy Coding instead directly targets representation structure, motivated by the hypothesis that the most generalizable plausible representation should have maximum entropy.

Directly optimizing entropy is computationally difficult, so the method uses a surrogate based on minimal coding length in lossy data coding. The authors derive a scalable reformulation that supports fast, end-to-end training. This turns an information-theoretic principle into a practical learning objective rather than leaving it as a conceptual preference.

Experiments report state-of-the-art results across linear probing, semi-supervised classification, detection, instance segmentation, and tracking. These findings support improved transfer across the evaluated tasks. The paper also shows that existing objectives organized around batches or features can be understood as low-order approximations of MEC. That connection places several learning objectives within a shared formulation while keeping maximum-entropy generalizability as the motivating hypothesis.
neurips-2022-self-supervised-learning-vi.tldr: Maximum Entropy Coding uses a tractable information-theoretic objective to learn representations with strong transfer across several downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Community detection seeks hidden groups from the pattern of connections among objects. A hypergraph allows a connection to involve more than two objects, and a stochastic block model describes random connections influenced by group membership. The paper studies when those connections contain enough information to recover meaningful community structure in a sparse hypergraph.

For the case of two groups, the authors establish the positive side of a conjectured sharp threshold. Above that threshold, non-trivial reconstruction is possible. The argument compares the community-structured hypergraph model with its Erdős–Rényi counterpart, using methods generalized from earlier work on sparse random graphs.

The paper also obtains estimates of the stochastic block model's parameters and discusses the negative side of the conjecture, where reconstruction would be impossible. The distinction matters: the stated theorem establishes possibility above the threshold for two groups, while impossibility is discussed rather than claimed as fully resolved. The result therefore advances a precise characterization of when sparse higher-order connections can reveal hidden communities.
neurips-2022-sparse-hypergraph-community.tldr: For two-community sparse hypergraph block models, the paper proves non-trivial reconstruction is possible above a conjectured threshold.

paragraphs: Transformations can be characterized by quantities they preserve. Distances, inner products, and angles provide examples for different transformation groups. The paper uses this observation to structure learned representations: when an input is transformed, corresponding invariant quantities in its representation should remain constant even though the representation itself may change.

This offers a route to learning equivariant representations without knowing the possibly nonlinear way the group acts on the input space. The authors use invariants as a symmetry regularizer on the latent representation instead of imposing them as hard constraints. Equivariance is guaranteed through other means, so regularization shapes the representation without carrying the entire guarantee.

The paper also demonstrates the feasibility of learning disentangled representations with this approach. Qualitative and quantitative results are favorable on downstream tasks including world modeling and reinforcement learning. Its central contribution is a way to use knowledge of preserved quantities to organize latent structure, connecting an abstract description of symmetry to representations that can support practical learning tasks.
neurips-2022-structuring-representations.tldr: Group invariants provide a symmetry regularizer for learning structured, equivariant representations without knowing the group's full input-space action.

paragraphs: A single aesthetic score compresses a person's response to a photograph, while a written critique can describe what they like and why. This paper introduces the Reddit Photo Critique Dataset to support studying that richer feedback. It contains 74,000 images and 220,000 comments from a photography community offering constructive criticism.

The dataset pairs photographs with comments that address different aspects of their appearance. Most images are UltraHD, and an automatic collection pipeline allows the dataset to grow. These properties make it a resource for connecting detailed language about photographs with the visual material being assessed, while acknowledging that aesthetic judgment is subjective.

The authors also investigate estimating aesthetic quality from critiques. They use sentiment polarity as an indicator of judgment and find a positive correlation with aesthetic judgments in two assessment benchmarks. They then train several models to rank images using sentiment scores as targets. The findings support sentiment as a useful source of aesthetic supervision, with the reported relationship being a positive correlation rather than an equivalence between sentiment and aesthetic quality.
neurips-2022-understanding-aesthetics-wi.tldr: A large photo-critique dataset supports learning aesthetic rankings from language, with critique sentiment positively correlated with benchmark aesthetic judgments.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can represent nonlinear relationships, yet they sometimes improve only slightly over linear models for node classification. This paper investigates that pattern through Bayesian inference. It asks which nonlinear operations arise when estimating a node's label from its own attributes and the attributes of its neighbors.

For graphs generated by a contextual stochastic block model, the authors identify two nonlinear parts in maximum-a-posteriori label estimation. One transforms node attributes; the other aggregates neighboring features using a ReLU activation. The latter resembles an operation already used in many graph neural networks, connecting their design to a statistical inference procedure.

Under an additional Gaussian assumption on node attributes, the authors prove that the ReLU advantage is significant only when attributes are far more informative than graph structure. They derive a similar argument for shifts in attribute distributions between training and testing. Synthetic and real-network experiments support the theory. The result gives a conditional explanation for modest nonlinear gains, grounded in how information is divided between attributes and connections.
neurips-2022-understanding-non-linearity.tldr: A Bayesian analysis explains when nonlinear neighbor aggregation offers significant advantages over linear graph models under stated statistical assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper builds explanations into image classification before the prediction is made. Its two architectures compare a query image with training examples and expose visual correspondences between them. The aim is to support both reliable classification and human judgment about whether a prediction should be accepted.

The models first rank training images using whole-image deep features. They then rerank the top 50 candidates using the five most similar patch pairs for each candidate. On ImageNet-related evaluations, out-of-distribution accuracy improves by one to four points, while ImageNet accuracy falls by one to two points relative to the stated ResNet-50 baseline. A similar pattern appears on CUB.

Human studies find that correspondence explanations improve both human-alone and human-AI team accuracy relative to k-nearest-neighbor explanations. They also help users correctly reject wrong AI decisions more often than all other tested methods. In both classification tasks, team accuracy can exceed either participant alone. These results connect localized visual evidence with complementary human-AI decisions while documenting an in-distribution accuracy tradeoff.
neurips-2022-visual-correspondence-based.tldr: Classifiers that explain predictions through matching image patches improve reported robustness and help human-AI teams outperform either participant alone.

paragraphs: Generating images from a three-dimensional scene often requires repeatedly querying a neural network along each viewing ray, which makes rendering slow. Some systems accelerate this by rendering coarse features and upsampling them, but camera changes can then unintentionally alter object geometry or appearance. VoxGRAF investigates a sparse voxel representation to address speed and consistency together.

The method replaces a monolithic coordinate-based network with three-dimensional convolutions. It combines sparse voxel grids with progressive growing, removal of empty space, and suitable regularization. The foreground object is represented in three dimensions, while the background is represented in two, keeping the scene compact and allowing higher voxel resolutions.

A single forward pass generates the full scene representation, which can then be rendered from arbitrary viewpoints efficiently. The reported results demonstrate high visual fidelity and three-dimensional consistency. The contribution is a generative representation that makes scene construction available upfront, reducing the need for repeated network queries while supporting coherent changes of viewpoint.
neurips-2022-voxgraf-fast-3d-aware-image.tldr: VoxGRAF generates sparse voxel scenes in one forward pass for fast, visually faithful, viewpoint-consistent rendering.
